1: # Polling Application
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: 
5: A **Polling Application** is an application for creating polls — small question instruments with predefined answer options — distributing them to a group through a low-friction participation path, and computing an aggregate result of the votes. The aggregate, not the individual responses, is the poll's deliverable: the poll exists to produce a shared answer to a question ("which option does the group prefer?"), not records to be processed afterwards.
6: 
7: The defining structure is small:
8: 
9: ```text
10: Poll (question + predefined answer options)
11: └── Lightweight distributed voting (a single act per participant)
12:     └── Computed vote aggregate (counts/percentages per option)
13: ```
14: 
15: Everything commonly associated with online polls — anonymous participation, live-updating charts, QR codes, duplicate-vote protection, comments, exports — is standard in mature products but is not what makes the product a polling application. Older and differently hosted forms (a question sheet on a noticeboard with tally marks, a show of hands with counted results) satisfy the same structure without any of the modern machinery.
16: 
17: When the product's center shifts — to a facilitator-run live session, to persisted per-submission records, to multi-question measurement instruments, or to finding a time for one occasion — it is drifting toward a different Application Type (Audience Response System, Online Form Builder, Survey Platform, Group Availability Scheduling).
18: 
19: ## Users & Context
20: 
21: The primary user is an **owner** (poll creator): anyone who needs a quick group decision or a read of group opinion — a friend planning an outing, a colleague choosing between options in a team channel, a presenter taking a quick audience temperature, a community moderator settling a question, a teacher asking a class to vote. Creating a poll is a self-service act that takes moments and, in the default case, no payment and no technical setup.
22: 
23: The second user is the **participant**: a member of the group the poll reaches. Participants typically need no account — they follow a link, click an option in a chat message, or scan a code, and their vote joins the aggregate. Identification, when required at all, is usually a self-declared name; anonymity is a common default.
24: 
25: A third, lighter role appears in organizational deployments: the **team or admin** who owns recurring polls and reads results across a workspace or dashboard.
26: 
27: The context is informal and ephemeral: polls are created in seconds, live for hours or days, answer one question, and end. The unit of work is one poll, not a program of measurement.
28: 
29: ## Core Model
30: 
31: ### The Defining Core
32: 
33: ```text
34: Poll (question + predefined answer options)
35: └── Lightweight distributed voting
36:     └── Computed vote aggregate
37: ```
38: 
39: Three properties. If any one is removed, the product is no longer recognizable as a polling application:
40: 
41: - **The poll as a small question instrument** — a stored, shareable object posing a question (typically one, at most a few) with a predefined set of answer options. The instrument is deliberately small: one click or tap answers it. Without a structured question-and-options object, there is nothing to vote on.
42: - **Lightweight distributed voting** — participants record their choice(s) through a shared participation path (link, embed, chat command, QR code, meeting surface) without needing accounts in the default case. The participation act is a single lightweight selection, not a form fill. Without distribution and voting, there is no poll; without lightness, it becomes a form.
43: - **The computed vote aggregate as the defining output** — the system tallies choices into an aggregate result per option, commonly shown as counts and percentages with a chart. The poll is finished when the aggregate has answered the question. Without the aggregate, the product is just answer collection.
44: 
45: ### Standard Capabilities
46: 
47: A typical modern polling product carries most of these capabilities. They make polls trustworthy and practical; they do not define the Type.
48: 
49: - **Shareable participation path** — a short link as the standard channel, extended by website embeds, QR codes for in-room display, and social/messenger share buttons.
50: - **Accountless participation as the default** — anyone with the link can vote; identity requirements (enter your name, registered users only, one-time invitation links) are settings the owner can turn on.
51: - **Vote-type catalog** — single-choice and multiple-choice are the base; ratings (star scales), rankings, dot voting and similar weightings are common extensions. Catalogs differ per product.
52: - **Results surface** — counts/percentages per option, charted (bar or pie), typically updating live as votes arrive and remaining viewable during and after the poll.
53: - **Lifecycle machinery** — optional deadlines and manual closing; open polls may run indefinitely until closed.
54: - **Integrity machinery** — duplicate-vote detection (address- or cookie-based), bot and VPN filtering, CAPTCHA-class checks, unique vote tokens or one-time links where tighter control is needed.
55: - **Owner management surface** — separate from the participant surface: edit the question or options, change settings, close or reopen, delete, control sharing rights, export results.
56: - **Discussion** — comments attached to the poll, commonly gated on participation or an account.
57: 
58: ### One Structure, Many Implementations
59: 
60: The core model is written in conceptual terms. Products realize each concept differently:
61: 
62: ```text
63: Concept:      The poll object
64: Realizations: a web poll at a hosted URL; a chat-platform object created by a command
65:               inside Slack/Teams; an option-type configuration in a decision tool
66:               (text, image, or date options)
67: 
68: Concept:      The participation path
69: Realizations: short link, website embed, QR code, Discord/chat bot command,
70:               in-channel button, meeting-app surface, web voting link combined
71:               with in-channel voting
72: 
73: Concept:      Participant identity
74: Realizations: fully anonymous; self-declared name; optional account;
75:               platform account of the chat/meeting tool; one-time invitation links
76: 
77: Concept:      The aggregate
78: Realizations: live chart on the poll page; results dashboard in the collaboration
79:               tool; exportable tables; who-voted-what listing when identity is recorded
80: ```
81: 
82: A reader who has only seen link-based web polls should be able to recognize chat-native polls, and vice versa, from the core model.
83: 
84: ## How It Works
85: 
86: ### The core loop
87: 
88: ```text
89: Compose the poll
90: → pose the question
91: → define the answer options (fixed set, or participants may add options)
92: → choose vote semantics (single choice, multiple choice, rating, ranking)
93: → set participation rules (open link vs named vs invited; deadline optional)
94: → distribute (share the link / post the command or embed / show the QR code)
95: → participants vote (each a single lightweight act)
96: → read and share the aggregate (live during, and after, the poll)
97: → close the poll (deadline reached or manual close)
98: ```
99: 
100: The loop is the same whether the poll lives on a standalone website or inside a chat channel — only the distribution surface changes. The product's own documentation across the sampled market describes exactly this sequence: create the question and options, send participants a link, wait for the votes, share the result.
101: 
102: ### Managing a live poll
103: 
104: The owner works from an admin surface separate from the participant view: edit the question or options while the poll runs, adjust settings, extend or set a deadline, close the poll, manage who may edit, delete the poll, and export the results. Polls without deadlines run indefinitely; closing ends voting but preserves the aggregate.
105: 
106: ### Keeping the vote honest
107: 
108: Because participation is open and lightweight, integrity is a first-class concern. Mature products control duplicate voting (by address, cookie, or device), filter bots and anonymizing services, run background human-verification checks, and offer stronger paths — named participation, registered users only, one-time links, unique vote tokens — for polls where manipulation matters. Products are explicit that result reliability depends on these settings: a loosely configured open poll is an informal signal, not a verified measurement.
109: 
110: ### Reading the results
111: 
112: The aggregate is the destination: a per-option tally, charted, viewable in real time. When participants are identified, a who-voted-what listing is typically available alongside the aggregate. When anonymity governs, only the aggregate is exposed. Results are meant to be shared — the owner passes the result link, chart, or export back to the group, which is frequently the poll's whole point.
113: 
114: ## Interfaces
115: 
116: The following surfaces are described conceptually; exact layouts and names vary by product.
117: 
118: ### Creation form (owner)
119: 
120: The owner's entry surface.
121: 
122: - question/title field, description, option list editor, vote-semantics selection, participation and deadline settings
123: - primary actions: add/remove options, toggle identity requirements, set deadline, create the poll
124: 
125: ### Participant voting page (or object)
126: 
127: What participants see — the poll's public face.
128: 
129: - the question, the option set, the vote control (a click/tap per choice), optional name field or comment box
130: - primary actions: select option(s), submit; in some products, add a new option or comment
131: 
132: ### Results view
133: 
134: The aggregate surface.
135: 
136: - per-option counts/percentages, chart, total participation; who-voted-what listing when identity is recorded
137: - primary actions: refresh/watch live, share the result, export
138: 
139: ### Admin / management surface
140: 
141: The owner's control panel over open and past polls.
142: 
143: - list of owned polls; per-poll edit, close/reopen, deadline, visibility and sharing rights, delete, export
144: - in platform-native products this surface is partly inside the collaboration tool (dashboard alongside in-channel results)
145: 
146: ### Host surfaces (platform-native products)
147: 
148: In chat- and meeting-native realizations, the poll is composed and answered inside commands, message objects, and meeting-app panels rather than a standalone site; the participant act stays a single click in place.
149: 
150: ## Important Rules / Behaviors
151: 
152: ### Identity is a settings axis, not a default
153: 
154: The same product may run fully anonymous polls, name-required polls, and registered-only polls. Identity changes what the results expose (aggregate only vs who-voted-what) and how strongly duplicates can be controlled — but the poll works identically in all postures.
155: 
156: ### Open participation means controlled trust
157: 
158: The default "anyone with the link can vote" model is intentionally low-friction; the integrity machinery (duplicate checks, filters, tokens) is how the owner tightens it when the stakes rise. Products state plainly that results are only as reliable as the chosen parameters — polls are informal signals by design, not verified measurement.
159: 
160: ### The poll has a simple lifecycle
161: 
162: A poll is created open (or opened on schedule), accepts votes until a deadline or manual close, and ends with a preserved aggregate. There is no approval chain, no per-response processing, no post-close workflow — the result ends the story.
163: 
164: ### Vote mutability varies by product
165: 
166: Whether a participant can change or withdraw a vote is a product rule, commonly conditioned on identity (an anonymous vote cannot be re-found; a named one can be edited). Option sets may be editable mid-poll by the owner, and some products let participants add options.
167: 
168: ### The aggregate is the deliverable
169: 
170: Response-level data may be retained (vote lists, editable entries, export files), but no part of the workflow is built around processing individual submissions. A product whose center is the per-response record — intake, routing, downstream handling — has left this Type.
171: 
172: ## Variants
173: 
174: Common realizations of the same core:
175: 
176: - **Standalone web poll maker** — a hosted service where the poll is a URL: create, share a link, watch the aggregate (consumer tier, commonly free/ad-funded).
177: - **Collaboration-platform-native polls** — the poll object lives inside a chat or meeting tool (created by command, answered in-channel or in-meeting, results in the same thread or a dashboard); participation friction is the design driver (business tier).
178: - **Multi-mode decision tools** — a family where the voting poll is one type beside surveys, tables/list collection, idea collection, and contests; the poll core is unchanged but packaged with adjacent modes.
179: - **Recurring / engagement polls** — scheduled and repeated polls with reminders and accumulating trend data in organizations (an extension toward engagement measurement).
180: - **Embedded polls** — native poll features inside meeting platforms, social networks, and forum software. These share the poll object but are capabilities of their container products, not standalone instances of this Type.
181: 
182: A variant stays a variant unless it changes the users, core objects, workflow or rules so much that the defining core no longer applies — as happens when polls accumulate into measurement programs (survey territory) or options become times for one occasion (scheduling territory).
183: 
184: ## Related Application Types
185: 
186: | Application Type | Distinction |
187: |---|---|
188: | Audience Response System | a facilitator-run live session container: mass participants join a room and the aggregate is displayed back to that same room while it happens; a poll is a shareable object without a host, a room, or a join act |
189: | Online Form Builder | a multi-field instrument whose defining output is the persisted per-submission record that the owner views, exports, and routes; a poll's defining output is the aggregate, and one click answers it |
190: | Survey Platform | an instrument battery tuned for measurement, with analysis and reporting as the deliverable; a poll is a single lightweight question with an instant tally — poll makers themselves disclaim scientific representativeness |
191: | Group Availability Scheduling Application | a time-finding poll for one occasion: options are candidate times, answers are availability declarations, and the endpoint is one chosen time; a generic poll tool can host a date poll, but the scheduling loop defines that Type |
192: | Questionnaire Application | sibling in the same directory family; the instrument/collection seam with forms and surveys is decided at that Type's own pass |
193: | Meeting / Webinar Platforms, Social Networks, Forum Software | their native poll features are embedded capabilities of those container products, not instances of this Type; the primary-surface test decides |
194: | Employee Survey Platform | measurement programs over a workforce population with confidentiality machinery; recurring polls that accumulate into engagement measurement drift toward it |
195: | Idea / Feedback Collection | open-text collection with upvoting lacks the predefined-option instrument and the computed aggregate |
196: 
197: The closest overlaps are the Audience Response System and the Online Form Builder: the session container separates polling from live audience response, and the output object (aggregate vs per-submission records) separates polling from form building.
198: 
199: ## Representative Products
200: 
201: - StrawPoll — standalone web poll maker, anonymous-first, free with ad-funding
202: - PollUnit — standalone freemium decision tool with votings as one mode beside tables, surveys and contests
203: - Polly — collaboration-platform-native polls for Slack, Teams and meeting tools (business tier)
204: 
205: The definition was also checked against platform-native and embedded realizations (chat bots, meeting-platform and social-network polls, forum poll threads) to avoid over-fitting to the standalone web-poll pattern.
206: 
207: ## Sources
208: 
209: Research date: **2026-09-08**
210: 
211: - StrawPoll — homepage, F.A.Q. and First Steps guide: https://strawpoll.com/ , https://strawpoll.com/help/faq/ , https://strawpoll.com/help/first-steps/
212: - PollUnit — homepage and "Create your first poll" tutorial: https://pollunit.com/en , https://pollunit.com/en/tutorials/create_your_first_poll
213: - Polly — homepage and Polls & Surveys product page: https://www.polly.ai/ , https://www.polly.ai/polls-and-surveys
214: 
215: > Sourcing limitations: Polly's evidence is product-page tier; its help-center articles were not fetched, so creation mechanics, anonymity option details and per-question-type behavior are described only where the product pages state them. One standalone free-poll product (Xoyondo) was unreachable (access denied) and is recorded as market context only. Precise operational details — participant limits, vote-token lifetimes, exact duplicate-check parameters, retention defaults — are intentionally not asserted anywhere in this document.
216: 
217: Detailed product-by-product observations, the cross-product comparison matrix, boundary analyses against neighboring Types, and the historical check are recorded in the paired Research Notes.

82: A reader who has only seen link-based web polls should be able to recognize chat-native polls, and vice versa, from the core model.
83: 
84: ## How It Works
85: 
86: ### The core loop
87: 
88: ```text
89: Compose the poll
90: → pose the question
91: → define the answer options (fixed set, or participants may add options)
92: → choose vote semantics (single choice, multiple choice, rating, ranking)
93: → set participation rules (open link vs named vs invited; deadline optional)
94: → distribute (share the link / post the command or embed / show the QR code)
95: → participants vote (each a single lightweight act)
96: → read and share the aggregate (live during, and after, the poll)
97: → close the poll (deadline reached or manual close)
98: ```
99: 
100: The loop is the same whether the poll lives on a standalone website or inside a chat channel — only the distribution surface changes. The product's own documentation across the sampled market describes exactly this sequence: create the question and options, send participants a link, wait for the votes, share the result.
101: 
102: ### Managing a live poll
103: 
104: The owner works from an admin surface separate from the participant view: edit the question or options while the poll runs, adjust settings, extend or set a deadline, close the poll, manage who may edit, delete the poll, and export the results. Polls without deadlines run indefinitely; closing ends voting but preserves the aggregate.
105: 
106: ### Keeping the vote honest
107: 
108: Because participation is open and lightweight, integrity is a first-class concern. Mature products control duplicate voting (by address, cookie, or device), filter bots and anonymizing services, run background human-verification checks, and offer stronger paths — named participation, registered users only, one-time links, unique vote tokens — for polls where manipulation matters. Products are explicit that result reliability depends on these settings: a loosely configured open poll is an informal signal, not a verified measurement.
109: 
110: ### Reading the results
111: 
112: The aggregate is the destination: a per-option tally, charted, viewable in real time. When participants are identified, a who-voted-what listing is typically available alongside the aggregate. When anonymity governs, only the aggregate is exposed. Results are meant to be shared — the owner passes the result link, chart, or export back to the group, which is frequently the poll's whole point.
113: 
114: ## Interfaces
115: 
116: The following surfaces are described conceptually; exact layouts and names vary by product.
117: 
118: ### Creation form (owner)
119: 
120: The owner's entry surface.
121: 
122: - question/title field, description, option list editor, vote-semantics selection, participation and deadline settings
123: - primary actions: add/remove options, toggle identity requirements, set deadline, create the poll
124: 
125: ### Participant voting page (or object)
126: 
127: What participants see — the poll's public face.
128: 
129: - the question, the option set, the vote control (a click/tap per choice), optional name field or comment box
130: - primary actions: select option(s), submit; in some products, add a new option or comment
131: 
132: ### Results view
133: 
134: The aggregate surface.
135: 
136: - per-option counts/percentages, chart, total participation; who-voted-what listing when identity is recorded
137: - primary actions: refresh/watch live, share the result, export
138: 
139: ### Admin / management surface
140: 
141: The owner's control panel over open and past polls.
142: 
143: - list of owned polls; per-poll edit, close/reopen, deadline, visibility and sharing rights, delete, export
144: - in platform-native products this surface is partly inside the collaboration tool (dashboard alongside in-channel results)
145: 
146: ### Host surfaces (platform-native products)
147: 
148: In chat- and meeting-native realizations, the poll is composed and answered inside commands, message objects, and meeting-app panels rather than a standalone site; the participant act stays a single click in place.
149: 
150: ## Important Rules / Behaviors
151: 
152: ### Identity is a settings axis, not a default
153: 
154: The same product may run fully anonymous polls, name-required polls, and registered-only polls. Identity changes what the results expose (aggregate only vs who-voted-what) and how strongly duplicates can be controlled — but the poll works identically in all postures.
155: 
156: ### Open participation means controlled trust
157: 
158: The default "anyone with the link can vote" model is intentionally low-friction; the integrity machinery (duplicate checks, filters, tokens) is how the owner tightens it when the stakes rise. Products state plainly that results are only as reliable as the chosen parameters — polls are informal signals by design, not verified measurement.
159: 
160: ### The poll has a simple lifecycle
161: 
162: A poll is created open (or opened on schedule), accepts votes until a deadline or manual close, and ends with a preserved aggregate. There is no approval chain, no per-response processing, no post-close workflow — the result ends the story.
163: 
164: ### Vote mutability varies by product
165: 
166: Whether a participant can change or withdraw a vote is a product rule, commonly conditioned on identity (an anonymous vote cannot be re-found; a named one can be edited). Option sets may be editable mid-poll by the owner, and some products let participants add options.
167: 
168: ### The aggregate is the deliverable
169: 
170: Response-level data may be retained (vote lists, editable entries, export files), but no part of the workflow is built around processing individual submissions. A product whose center is the per-response record — intake, routing, downstream handling — has left this Type.
171: 
172: ## Variants
173: 
174: Common realizations of the same core:
175: 
176: - **Standalone web poll maker** — a hosted service where the poll is a URL: create, share a link, watch the aggregate (consumer tier, commonly free/ad-funded).
177: - **Collaboration-platform-native polls** — the poll object lives inside a chat or meeting tool (created by command, answered in-channel or in-meeting, results in the same thread or a dashboard); participation friction is the design driver (business tier).
178: - **Multi-mode decision tools** — a family where the voting poll is one type beside surveys, tables/list collection, idea collection, and contests; the poll core is unchanged but packaged with adjacent modes.
179: - **Recurring / engagement polls** — scheduled and repeated polls with reminders and accumulating trend data in organizations (an extension toward engagement measurement).
180: - **Embedded polls** — native poll features inside meeting platforms, social networks, and forum software. These share the poll object but are capabilities of their container products, not standalone instances of this Type.
181: 
182: A variant stays a variant unless it changes the users, core objects, workflow or rules so much that the defining core no longer applies — as happens when polls accumulate into measurement programs (survey territory) or options become times for one occasion (scheduling territory).
183: 
184: ## Related Application Types
185: 
186: | Application Type | Distinction |
187: |---|---|
188: | Audience Response System | a facilitator-run live session container: mass participants join a room and the aggregate is displayed back to that same room while it happens; a poll is a shareable object without a host, a room, or a join act |
189: | Online Form Builder | a multi-field instrument whose defining output is the persisted per-submission record that the owner views, exports, and routes; a poll's defining output is the aggregate, and one click answers it |
190: | Survey Platform | an instrument battery tuned for measurement, with analysis and reporting as the deliverable; a poll is a single lightweight question with an instant tally — poll makers themselves disclaim scientific representativeness |
191: | Group Availability Scheduling Application | a time-finding poll for one occasion: options are candidate times, answers are availability declarations, and the endpoint is one chosen time; a generic poll tool can host a date poll, but the scheduling loop defines that Type |
192: | Questionnaire Application | sibling in the same directory family; the instrument/collection seam with forms and surveys is decided at that Type's own pass |
193: | Meeting / Webinar Platforms, Social Networks, Forum Software | their native poll features are embedded capabilities of those container products, not instances of this Type; the primary-surface test decides |
194: | Employee Survey Platform | measurement programs over a workforce population with confidentiality machinery; recurring polls that accumulate into engagement measurement drift toward it |
195: | Idea / Feedback Collection | open-text collection with upvoting lacks the predefined-option instrument and the computed aggregate |
196: 
197: The closest overlaps are the Audience Response System and the Online Form Builder: the session container separates polling from live audience response, and the output object (aggregate vs per-submission records) separates polling from form building.
198: 
199: ## Representative Products
200: 
201: - StrawPoll — standalone web poll maker, anonymous-first, free with ad-funding
202: - PollUnit — standalone freemium decision tool with votings as one mode beside tables, surveys and contests
203: - Polly — collaboration-platform-native polls for Slack, Teams and meeting tools (business tier)
204: 
205: The definition was also checked against platform-native and embedded realizations (chat bots, meeting-platform and social-network polls, forum poll threads) to avoid over-fitting to the standalone web-poll pattern.
206: 
207: ## Sources
208: 
209: Research date: **2026-09-08**
210: 
211: - StrawPoll — homepage, F.A.Q. and First Steps guide: https://strawpoll.com/ , https://strawpoll.com/help/faq/ , https://strawpoll.com/help/first-steps/
212: - PollUnit — homepage and "Create your first poll" tutorial: https://pollunit.com/en , https://pollunit.com/en/tutorials/create_your_first_poll
213: - Polly — homepage and Polls & Surveys product page: https://www.polly.ai/ , https://www.polly.ai/polls-and-surveys
214: 
215: > Sourcing limitations: Polly's evidence is product-page tier; its help-center articles were not fetched, so creation mechanics, anonymity option details and per-question-type behavior are described only where the product pages state them. One standalone free-poll product (Xoyondo) was unreachable (access denied) and is recorded as market context only. Precise operational details — participant limits, vote-token lifetimes, exact duplicate-check parameters, retention defaults — are intentionally not asserted anywhere in this document.
216: 
217: Detailed product-by-product observations, the cross-product comparison matrix, boundary analyses against neighboring Types, and the historical check are recorded in the paired Research Notes.
